strengths: The paper offers a useful mechanistic contribution: DiTs with similar task performance can route spatial information differently depending on their text encoder. The distinction between explicit relation-reading heads with random embeddings and contextual information carried by object tokens with T5 is relevant to understanding text-to-image generation.

The RTE analysis goes beyond attention visualization. Relation-token ablation in L2H8 reduces relational accuracy from 67% to 33%, while object-token ablation in L4H3 reduces shape accuracy from 90% to 76%. The positional QK analysis and VO-injection experiment provide complementary support for a relation-to-object pathway.

The T5 experiments triangulate contextual information routing through token masking, variance partitioning, and embedding interventions. Changing a relation component in the second object's embedding changes generated geometry, supporting a causal role for information carried by that token.

The prompt-sensitivity result is substantial and informative. In Table 2, adding 'the' reduces T5 DiT-B spatial accuracy from 0.808 to 0.498 while binding accuracy improves; RTE DiT-B remains stable at 0.843 versus 0.862. Similar behavior in DiT-mini strengthens this observation. The synthetic setting enables interpretable evaluation without requiring benchmark-leading image quality.
weaknesses: The evidence supports influential components more strongly than the claimed 'minimal circuit.' Head ablations establish contributions, but the VO-injection experiment demonstrates downstream attention selectivity rather than successful image generation from the isolated circuit. The pathway for the second object, which involves several relation-attending heads, is not comparably resolved. Circuit sufficiency and completeness therefore remain unestablished.

The T5 causal evidence is narrow relative to the claim of a general alternative circuit. Figure 8 illustrates token masking for one prompt and one relation-vector transformation, without aggregate intervention success or attribute-preservation rates across relations and object combinations. Shape-token ablation also damages object recognition and binding, so the accompanying spatial-score decrease does not independently isolate relational processing. Table 1's additive model explains only 53.4% of projected-representation variance, limiting the proposed factorization.

The dataset description contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3 specifies eight relations and noncolliding objects, whereas Appendix B.1 and its pseudocode include occlusion, 'in front of,' and 'behind.' The appendix also fixes the first captioned object to red and the second to blue, while analyzed examples reverse this assignment. These differences affect which shortcuts are available and whether evaluated prompts are in distribution; they prevent a confident reconstruction of the experimental setting.

Evaluation protocols and headline claims are insufficiently reconciled. The abstract says all models reach near-perfect accuracy, but Table 2 reports roughly 81–84% loose spatial accuracy for the principal DiT-B models and much poorer results for smaller models. The manuscript uses 96, 168, and 264 prompt sets in different analyses without clearly mapping their composition to each result, and the 67% circuit-ablation baseline is not reconciled with the main evaluation. Independent training-seed counts and variability of the discovered circuits are also unclear.

The observed robustness difference is convincing within the tested templates, but its attribution to information fusion remains a hypothesis: the paper does not directly connect filler-induced embedding changes to circuit failure or demonstrate recovery through a targeted intervention. Extrapolation to text encoders being the bottleneck in real-world generation is therefore premature. Overall, the original mechanistic observations have clear value, but incomplete causal characterization and unresolved experimental-specification issues place the submission near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The controlled comparison of contextual T5 embeddings and fixed random embeddings reveals an interesting distinction in how DiTs implement spatial conditioning. This is a relevant interpretability contribution without requiring benchmark-leading generation performance.

The RTE analysis goes beyond attention visualization: positional-embedding QK maps, selective head ablations, and the VO injection experiment provide converging evidence for relation-sensitive and object-sensitive heads. The reported relation-accuracy decrease from 67% to 33% when ablating L2H8 is substantial.
For T5, token masking, variance partitioning, and embedding interventions support the narrower conclusion that contextual object-token embeddings carry usable spatial information.

The prompt-sensitivity result is substantial and supported across model sizes. Table 2 shows that adding 'the' reduces T5 DiT-B loose relation accuracy from 0.808 to 0.498 while binding accuracy improves; RTE DiT-B remains stable. This helps distinguish spatial failure from general image degradation.

The appendix provides extensive architectural, training, evaluation, and representation-analysis details, and attention synopsis offers a practical way to organize large collections of attention maps.
weaknesses: The evidence supports important circuit components more convincingly than a complete 'minimal circuit.' Figure 6 compares heads within the selected layers, and Figure 5C shows selective attention after a fivefold-scaled VO injection rather than recovery of correct generated relations. There is no end-to-end sufficiency or pathway-specific rescue test establishing that the proposed two-head chain explains generation; Figure 7 itself labels parts of the second-object and feature-writing mechanism hypothetical.

The T5 claim of reading relation and object information from a single token is stronger than demonstrated. Removing shape2 also damages shape and binding, which can itself lower the relation metric, while EOS removal collapses generation. Figure 8B provides an illustrative relation edit, but no aggregate editing success, identity-preservation statistics, or matched control directions establish the breadth and specificity of this mechanism.

The dataset specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3 describes eight relations with collision avoidance, whereas Appendix B.1 and its pseudocode include overlapping objects and two additional depth relations. The appendix also fixes the first-mentioned object to red and the second to blue. This creates a possible shortcut between color and sentence role that is not separated from the claimed object-independent mechanism.

The robustness difference is established, but its attribution to circuit disentanglement remains a hypothesis. The experiments do not isolate contextual-embedding changes from narrow-template training or demonstrate that modifying the identified mechanism changes robustness. The suggestion that text encoders are the primary bottleneck in real-world spatial generation therefore exceeds the evidence.

Performance reporting needs reconciliation. The abstract's near-perfect accuracy contrasts with Table 2's approximately 81–84% loose and 75–76% strict relation accuracy for DiT-B on the training template, and the RTE ablation starts at 67%. Evaluation pools also differ across sections without a clear mapping. Training-seed counts and replication of the identified circuits are insufficiently specified.

Overall, the mechanistic observations and robustness measurements make this a worthwhile submission, but incomplete causal validation and ambiguity in the experimental specification leave it near the acceptance boundary. The controlled synthetic setting is appropriate; the concern is whether the stated mechanisms are established within that setting.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting mechanistic contribution: comparable spatial-generation performance can arise through different pathways depending on the text encoder. The contrast between explicit relation-token processing with random embeddings and contextual information in T5 object tokens is relevant to understanding text-to-image models, independently of benchmark improvements.

The RTE analysis goes beyond attention visualization. Positional-embedding/QK analysis, selective attention ablations, and VO injection provide converging evidence for a relation-to-location pathway followed by object-token selection. The reported drop in relation accuracy from 67% to 33% when ablating L2H8 is substantial.

The T5 embedding interventions provide useful causal evidence that object-token representations carry actionable spatial information. Variance partitioning and relation-vector arithmetic complement the token-masking experiments.

The robustness difference is quantitatively compelling within this setting. Table 2 shows T5 DiT-B relation accuracy falling from 0.808 to 0.498 after adding 'the', while RTE DiT-B remains stable at 0.843 versus 0.862. Results across model sizes and detailed architecture, sampling, and evaluation descriptions strengthen the controlled study.
weaknesses: The evidence supports important circuit components more strongly than the claimed 'minimal circuit'. Figure 6 compares heads within the selected layers, rather than establishing circuit completeness across the network. Figure 5C injects a scaled relation-head output into positional embeddings and measures downstream attention; it does not demonstrate that the proposed two-head pathway is sufficient for correct generation or mediates the effect during ordinary denoising. The processing of the second object and other network components remains incompletely resolved.

The T5 mechanism is less fully localized. Figure 8A uses one displayed prompt, and masking shape2 impairs shape and binding as well as relation accuracy. Because relation evaluation depends on identifying correctly bound objects, this decrease does not isolate a specifically relational computation. The embedding edit is persuasive as an example, but aggregate intervention success, identity preservation, and controls across source/target relations are not reported. Consequently, the strong claim that generation reads all required information from a single token exceeds the demonstrated evidence.

The dataset specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3 describes eight relations and noncolliding objects, whereas Appendix B.1 and its pseudocode include occlusion and front/behind relations. The appendix also fixes the first described object to red and the second to blue, while the main evaluation includes reversed color orders. If implemented as written, this introduces a color/order shortcut and changes which evaluations are in distribution. The manuscript does not reconcile these descriptions.

Evaluation reporting makes the scope of several claims difficult to establish. Section 3 uses 96 prompts, Appendix B.5 describes 168, and Table 2 uses 264 without clearly connecting these populations. The abstract's 'near-perfect' characterization is not representative of Table 2's roughly 81–84% loose relation accuracy and 75–76% stringent accuracy for DiT-B. Training-run counts and variability of the discovered circuits are also insufficiently documented; numerous sampling seeds do not establish reproducibility across independently trained models.

The prompt-robustness result establishes a behavioral difference, but its attribution to circuit disentanglement remains a hypothesis: the paper does not directly trace or rescue the failure caused by the added token. Extrapolation to text-encoder bottlenecks in realistic T2I systems is correspondingly tentative. Overall, the original controlled findings have clear value, but incomplete support for the central circuit claims and uncertainty about the actual training distribution place the submission at the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper offers a useful mechanistic contribution to text-to-image generation: it connects text-encoder choice to different pathways for constructing spatial layouts. Studying this in a controlled synthetic setting is scientifically valuable without requiring benchmark-leading performance.

The RTE analysis combines attention summaries, weight-space geometry, and interventions. Ablating L2H8 reduces relational accuracy from 67% to 33%, while ablating L4H3 reduces shape accuracy from 90% to 76%. These results support functional specialization beyond attention-map correlation alone.

The contextual-embedding analysis provides complementary evidence. Variance partitioning identifies relation information in the second shape token, and editing relation vectors changes generated spatial arrangements. The CLIP extension includes individual and joint head ablations, strengthening the evidence that the analysis is useful across encoders.

The prompt-sensitivity result is substantial and practically interesting. In Table 2, inserting 'the' before the second object reduces T5-DiT-B's loose relation accuracy from 0.808 to 0.498 while binding accuracy improves; RTE-DiT-B remains stable at 0.843 versus 0.862. This isolates a meaningful spatial failure rather than merely degraded image quality.

Attention Synopsis and weight-space screening provide interpretable procedures for narrowing a large search over heads and diffusion steps. The appendix supplies substantial architectural, evaluation, and mathematical detail, and the multi-scale experiments broaden the controlled study.
weaknesses: The evidence supports influential components more strongly than a complete 'minimal circuit.' Individual ablations establish contribution, but do not demonstrate that the proposed two-head pathway is sufficient for generation. Figure 5C injects a scaled relation-head output into positional embeddings and measures downstream attention, rather than restoring spatial behavior through the proposed path in the running model. Figure 6 itself labels parts of the second-object and value-output mechanism hypothetical. T5's selected L3H7 is screened geometrically without a corresponding targeted head-ablation result.

The proposed explanation connecting contextual information fusion to brittleness is underdetermined by the paper's own CLIP results. Appendix A.9 finds similar reliance on object-token embeddings, yet CLIP remains comparatively robust to filler-word perturbations. This supports a T5-specific representation/decoder mismatch, but not a general robustness disadvantage of the contextual circuit. A causal correction of the perturbation-induced relation component is not demonstrated.

Important dataset details conflict. Section 3 describes eight spatial relations and collision avoidance, whereas Appendix B.1 and its pseudocode include overlapping objects and front/behind captions. The appendix also fixes the first described object to red and the second to blue, while evaluation includes both color orders. These ambiguities affect whether color/order shortcuts are available and which evaluations are actually in distribution; they are more consequential than editorial inconsistencies.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated evaluation. Table 2 reports approximately 81–84% loose and 75–76% strict relation accuracy for the main DiT-B configurations, which does not substantiate the abstract's broad 'near-perfect' characterization. The manuscript also does not clearly reconcile these aggregate results with the 67% baseline used for the central RTE ablation. Figure 27D evaluates inversion and color synonyms only for T5, so it does not establish the stated comparative RTE advantage for those perturbations.

Transfer to realistic models remains preliminary. The PixArt-Sigma analysis screens heads and performs token masking on one selected high-performing prompt, but does not causally validate the screened heads. Consequently, identifying sparse spatial circuits in pretrained models—and prioritizing encoder improvements over DiT changes—remains suggestive rather than established.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed appendix: Section C provides no actual code or dataset link, training-seed replication of the discovered mechanisms is unclear, and the distinction between default weight decay and the separately labeled WD models is not adequately resolved. Overall, the original mechanistic observations and interventions place the paper near acceptance, but incomplete circuit validation and unresolved experimental definitions keep the current recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper provides a useful mechanistic contribution to understanding spatial composition in diffusion transformers. The controlled comparison identifies distinct ways of accessing relational information with random versus contextual text embeddings. This supported finding favors weak acceptance despite reservations about the broader interpretations.

The analysis goes beyond attention visualization. Ablating RTE head L2H8 reduces relational accuracy from 67% to 33%, while ablating L4H3 reduces shape accuracy from 90% to 76%. The VO injection experiment and T5 embedding interventions provide complementary evidence for the proposed information pathways (Figs. 4–7).

Attention Synopsis and weight-space screening form a practical, interpretable workflow for locating candidate spatial heads. Experiments across model sizes, and the additional CLIP analysis with individual and combined head ablations, strengthen the contribution beyond a single model example.

The prompt-robustness difference is substantial and well documented. Table 2 evaluates 264 prompts with 50 samples each: inserting 'the' before the second object changes T5-DiT-B relational accuracy from 0.808 to 0.498, while RTE-DiT-B remains stable. The appendix provides extensive architectural, optimization, evaluation, and factorization details.
weaknesses: The evidence supports important circuit components more strongly than a complete or minimal two-head circuit. The RTE ablations demonstrate partial necessity, while Fig. 5C demonstrates selective attention under constructed inputs rather than restoration of correct image generation through the proposed pathway. The respective ablation plots compare heads within selected layers. An end-to-end sufficiency or path-specific mediation experiment is absent, leaving the roles of other heads, self-attention, and MLPs unresolved.

The explanation that contextual information fusion causes brittleness is not established generally. CLIP-DiT also extracts relational information primarily from object tokens, yet remains relatively robust to the tested template changes (A.9 and Table 2). This internal counterexample suggests that object-token decoding alone is insufficient to explain T5's failure. The observed embedding shifts support a T5-specific account, but no intervention selectively removes those shifts and demonstrates recovery.

Transfer to pretrained models remains preliminary. The PixArt-Sigma token-ablation analysis uses the highest-accuracy prompt, and weight-space screening identifies candidate heads without corresponding causal head ablations (A.10). These results demonstrate applicability of the diagnostic tools, but do not establish that the synthetic circuits explain spatial failures in realistic models or that text-encoder improvements should take priority over DiT changes.

Several performance and representation claims are stronger than the quantitative evidence. Table 2 reports in-template loose relational accuracy of 0.843 for RTE-DiT-B and 0.808 for T5-DiT-B, with strict scores near 0.75, qualifying the abstract's 'near-perfect' characterization. Likewise, the additive factor model explains 73.2% of T5 embedding variance and 53.4% after projection; this supports a useful approximation rather than complete factorization. Embedding-edit success is illustrated without aggregate success rates across relations and object pairs.

Reproducibility has concrete gaps despite the detailed appendix. Section C claims public availability but supplies no repository address. Section 3 describes noncolliding objects and eight relations, whereas B.1 explicitly includes occlusion and front/behind captions; the actual training distribution is therefore ambiguous. Training-run counts and variation in discovered circuits across independent initializations are also unclear. These reporting issues are correctable, but currently limit replication and assessment of circuit stability.

strengths: The paper makes a worthwhile mechanistic contribution: it explains how text-conditioned diffusion transformers can translate relational information into spatial gradients and object placement, and how this computation changes with the text encoder. This is valuable independently of benchmark improvements.

The RTE analysis combines attention visualization with causal interventions. Ablating L2H8 reduces relation accuracy from 67% to 33%, while ablating L4H3 reduces shape accuracy from 90% to 76%. Injecting the former head’s output into the latter’s query input provides additional evidence for the proposed sequential pathway (Figs. 4–5).

The contextual-encoder analysis goes beyond attention inspection. Token masking, variance partitioning, and relation-vector interventions support the finding that object-token embeddings carry usable relational information (Fig. 7). The CLIP experiments add targeted individual and joint head ablations (Fig. 29).

Attention Synopsis and weight-space screening provide useful, interpretable tools for narrowing the search over diffusion attention heads. Experiments across model sizes and three encoder families strengthen the contribution beyond a single illustrative model.

The prompt-robustness difference is substantial and well documented. In Table 2, inserting 'the' before the second object lowers T5-DiT-B’s loose relation accuracy from 0.808 to 0.498, while RTE-DiT-B remains stable. Overall, the controlled mechanistic evidence supports weak acceptance, despite limitations in circuit completeness and broader interpretation.
weaknesses: The evidence establishes important circuit components more convincingly than a complete 'minimal circuit.' Figure 5C demonstrates selective attention in a constructed head input, rather than end-to-end sufficiency or mediation of the proposed pathway during generation. The second-object pathway remains partly hypothetical in Fig. 6. For T5, embedding interventions establish that relational information is usable, but do not specifically establish the causal necessity of the screened L3H7 head.

The explanation linking contextual information fusion to brittleness is incomplete. CLIP uses a similar object-token-centered mechanism yet remains robust to the tested template changes (Appendix A.9 and Table 2). This internal counterexample shows that fusion alone does not explain T5’s failures. The observed embedding shifts are informative, but the manuscript does not isolate what distinguishes robust from brittle contextual circuits.

Evidence for transfer to pretrained models is preliminary. Appendix A.10 reports nontrivial performance for only 8 of 30 object pairs, performs token ablation on the highest-accuracy prompt, and identifies heads through weight-space screening without corresponding causal head interventions. This supports tool applicability more strongly than the claim that interpretable spatial circuits have been established in a pretrained model.

Some reported conclusions exceed the quantitative evidence. Table 2 gives standard-template loose relation accuracy of 0.843 for RTE-DiT-B and 0.808 for T5-DiT-B, with strict scores around 0.75, so the abstract’s 'near-perfect' characterization needs qualification. Spatial accuracy also requires correct object binding, meaning that simultaneous declines in binding and relation accuracy, particularly in CLIP ablations, do not by themselves establish relation-specific disruption.

Reproducibility is helped by extensive methodological detail but hindered by inconsistencies. Section 3 describes collision-free scenes with eight relations, whereas Appendix B.1 includes occlusions and front/behind labels and fixes the first captioned object to red and the second to blue. The actual training distribution and any color/order randomization are therefore unclear. Independent training-run counts and circuit variability are insufficiently specified, and Appendix C’s availability statement contains no link.
